title: Client-Server Architecture & Multiplexing
intro: The client-server model partitions workloads between resource providers (servers) and service requesters (clients), forming the bedrock of modern distributed applications.
objectives: Differentiate stateful vs stateless client-server architectures.
Evaluate HTTP/1.1 pipelining vs HTTP/2 binary framing vs HTTP/3 QUIC UDP multiplexing.
Design robust connection pooling and keep-alive socket reuse mechanisms.
body:
In a client-server architecture, clients initiate requests and servers process and respond. Modern high-scale architectures enforce **stateless servers**, storing session state externally in Redis or JWT tokens. This allows any server instance behind a load balancer to handle any client request, enabling trivial horizontal scaling.

### Transport Protocol Evolution
- **HTTP/1.1**: Text-based, head-of-line (HOL) blocking at the application level; requires opening multiple TCP connections in parallel.
- **HTTP/2**: Binary framing layer, multiplexes hundreds of concurrent requests over a single TCP stream. Still suffers from TCP-level HOL blocking on packet drop.
- **HTTP/3 (QUIC)**: Runs over UDP with built-in encryption and independent multiplexed streams, eliminating packet-loss head-of-line blocking completely.
keyIdea: Stateless servers make horizontal scaling trivial. Protocol multiplexing (HTTP/2 & HTTP/3) maximizes network throughput over single connection pipes.

concepts.title: Connection Pooling
concepts.body: Establishing TCP/TLS handshakes costs 3-4 RTTs. Persistent connection pools maintain idle pre-warmed sockets to slash P99 latency.

concepts.title: Head-of-Line Blocking
concepts.body: When an earlier packet delay holds up subsequent independent responses on the same TCP channel.

examples: Envoy reverse proxy multiplexing HTTP/2 upstream to Spring Boot services.
Browser HTTP/3 connection migration when switching from Wi-Fi to cellular.

quiz.prompt: Why does HTTP/3 operate over UDP instead of TCP?
options: To eliminate TCP-level head-of-line blocking on packet loss
UDP guarantees reliable packet delivery natively
quiz.explanation: QUIC/HTTP/3 runs over UDP so a lost packet in one stream does not pause other concurrent streams on the same connection.
